title: Special String Again
directAnswer: Count substrings that are 'special palindromes': either (a) all characters identical, or (b) all identical except a single different middle character. Run-length-encode the string into (char, count) runs. Type (a) contributes L·(L+1)/2 per run of length L. Type (b): for each single-character run (count == 1) whose neighbours are the same character, add min(left run length, right run length). Sum both. O(n) time, O(n) space.

rules: Type (a): a run of L equal chars yields `L·(L+1)/2` all-same substrings (sum 1..L).
Type (b) needs the middle run to be **exactly one** character (`count == 1`).
Type (b) requires the **left and right neighbour runs to be the same character**.
Type (b) contributes `min(left.count, right.count)` — limited by the shorter flanking run.
Single-character runs as the middle are the only valid 'odd one out'; longer middles can't center a special palindrome.
whenToUse: Count substrings defined by adjacency/run structure rather than arbitrary content
Same-character runs and their single-char separators drive the answer
An O(n) RLE pass replaces an O(n²) substring enumeration
Palindrome-like structure that's really 'a block of one char, maybe split by one other'
antiSignals: General palindromic substrings (any content) → expand-around-center / Manacher, not RLE
Order-independent counts → frequency map, not runs
Substrings must be contiguous AND arbitrary → different DP
You need the substrings themselves, not the count → enumerate explicitly
remember.takeaway: Run-length encoding turns this into arithmetic over runs. All-same substrings come from the triangular number of each run; the 'one odd middle' palindromes come from single-char runs flanked by equal characters, bounded by the shorter neighbour. No O(n²) scan needed.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you compress the string into runs and translate the two special-palindrome shapes into closed-form counts, avoiding the naive O(n²) (or worse) substring enumeration.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Counting type (b) with the wrong bound (using the middle or the larger neighbour instead of min of the two flanks), or requiring the middle run to be a single char but forgetting to check the neighbours are the same character.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive both formulas out loud: triangular number for all-same runs, and min(left,right) for a one-character separator between two equal-character runs. State it's a single O(n) pass after RLE.

problemStatement:
A string is a **special palindrome** if either:

1. **All** of its characters are the same (e.g. `"aaa"`), or
2. All characters **except the middle one** are the same, and the middle character differs (e.g. `"aadaa"`).

Given a string `s` of length `n`, count how many **substrings** of `s` are special palindromes (substrings at different positions count separately even if equal).
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
Count substrings by position — identical content at different indices counts multiple times
The answer can be large; use a 64-bit integer
understanding: Special palindromes have only two shapes. Shape one is a solid block of a single letter. Shape two is a block of one letter with a single different letter sitting exactly in the middle (so the block splits evenly on both sides). Both shapes are dictated entirely by runs of identical characters. Compress the string into runs, then count each shape with a formula instead of scanning every substring.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do substrings at different positions count separately?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Two equal substrings at different indices are counted twice — we count occurrences, not distinct strings.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the middle 'odd' character be more than one character?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. For shape two the middle must be exactly one differing character, so it comes from a single-character run flanked by equal-character runs.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What bounds the count of a shape-two palindrome?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The shorter of the two flanking runs, because the palindrome must extend equally on both sides of the single middle char — min(left, right).

clarifyingQuestions.question: How big can the answer get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: With n up to 10⁶ and triangular counts, the total can exceed 32-bit range — use long / 64-bit.

examples.explanation: Runs: m1,n1,o1,n1,o1,p1,o2. Type (a): six length-1 runs give 6, the o2 run gives 3 → 9. Type (b): o(between n,n)=1, n(between o,o)=1, p(between o,o)=min(1,2)=1 → 3. Total 12.
Single run a4. Type (a): 4·5/2 = 10. No type (b) candidates. Total 10.
Runs all length 1: a,s,a,s,d. Type (a): 5. Type (b): s between a,a → 1; a between s,s → 1; s between a,d → no. Total 5 + 2 = 7.

approaches.explanation:
The definitional approach: generate every substring and test whether it is a special palindrome (all same, or all same with one differing middle character), incrementing a counter on each success.

**Why it's correct.** It checks the literal definition on every candidate, so it can't miss any.

**Why it's unusable.** With `n` up to 10⁶ there are ~5·10¹¹ substrings — enumerating them is impossible, let alone validating each. The structure to exploit: special palindromes are entirely determined by *runs* of identical characters. Compressing to runs reduces the problem to a couple of arithmetic formulas over at most `n` runs.
approaches.insight: Both special-palindrome shapes are functions of run boundaries, not of individual character positions. Once you see that, the O(n²) substring space collapses to an O(n) walk over runs.

approaches.name: Run-Length Encoding with Closed-Form Counts (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer — RLE the string, then apply the triangular-number and min(left,right) formulas.
hints: Compress s into runs of identical characters: e.g. "aaabb" → [(a,3),(b,2)].
All-same substrings inside a run of length L number L·(L+1)/2 (choose any start≤end within the run).
For the 'one odd middle' shape, look at single-character runs whose left and right runs are the same character; they contribute min(leftLen, rightLen).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the run list is one O(n) pass. Summing triangular numbers and scanning runs for type (b) is O(number of runs) ≤ O(n). Total O(n) time; the run list is O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Run-length-encode `s` into a list of `(char, count)` runs, then count the two shapes with arithmetic.

**Type (a) — all identical.** Any substring lying entirely within a run of `L` equal characters is all-same. The number of substrings of a length-`L` block is `1 + 2 + … + L = L·(L+1)/2` (pick any start, any later-or-equal end). Sum that over all runs.

**Type (b) — one differing middle.** This shape is `XX…X Y XX…X` with equal arms of `X` around a single `Y`. In RLE terms that's a **single-character run** `(Y, 1)` whose **left and right neighbour runs share the same character** `X`. The palindrome must extend equally on both sides of `Y`, so its arm length can be at most the shorter of the two flanking runs — giving exactly `min(leftLen, rightLen)` distinct special palindromes centred on that `Y` (arm length 1, 2, …, up to the min).

**Why the middle run must be length 1.** Shape two allows only a *single* odd character. A middle run of length ≥ 2 would put two non-`X` characters in the centre, which no special palindrome permits.

**Why `min(left, right)` and not the middle or the max.** The arms must be equal length and made entirely of `X`. You can grow each arm only as far as its run lasts; the shorter run is the binding constraint, so the count of valid arm lengths is `min(leftLen, rightLen)`.

**Why O(n).** One pass builds the runs; one more pass counts. No substring is ever materialized or rescanned.

**Why 64-bit.** Triangular numbers over runs summing across 10⁶ characters can exceed the 32-bit range — accumulate in `long`.
approaches.insight: RLE is the right lens whenever a substring property depends only on blocks of identical characters and their single-character separators. The two formulas — triangular number per block, `min(neighbours)` per lone separator — are a reusable template for 'count special-shaped substrings' problems.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong bound for shape two
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A shape-two palindrome grows equally on both sides of the single middle char, so it's capped by the SHORTER flanking run. Using the larger run (or the middle) overcounts.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Middle run longer than one
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Shape two permits exactly one odd character. A middle run of length ≥ 2 means two non-matching characters in the centre, which is never a special palindrome.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if runs[k - 1][0] == runs[k + 1][0]:
    total += min(runs[k - 1][1], runs[k + 1][1])
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if runs[k][1] == 1 and runs[k - 1][0] == runs[k + 1][0]:
    total += min(runs[k - 1][1], runs[k + 1][1])

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer overflow on the total
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Triangular numbers summed over n = 10⁶ can exceed 2³¹. Accumulate in a 64-bit integer.

patternNote: Run-length encoding plus closed-form counting. When substring counts depend only on blocks of identical characters and lone separators, compress to runs and replace O(n²) enumeration with arithmetic: triangular numbers for solid blocks, min(left,right) for a single odd middle between equal neighbours.
